Who benefits: Consumers seeking convenient, hands-free hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., music, outdoor work, or construction).. Why behaviour changes: If a product provides a tangible benefit not available in existing alternatives, consumers will switch to it; otherwise, they will remain with current solutions.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for the differentiated feature (e.g., premium pricing for Bluetooth connectivity) and sell through consumer channels, capturing higher margins than standard protective gear.. T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it offers a clear functional advantage (e.g., wireless connectivity, superior comfort, or specific use-case functionality) that addresses their pain points, and they are willing to pay a premium for that advantage. Who benefits: Consumers seeking convenient, hands-free hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., outdoor enthusiasts, musicians, or workers).. Why behaviour changes: If a product provides a tangible benefit not available in existing alternatives, consumers will switch to it; otherwise, they will remain with current solutions.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by pricing at a premium (e.g., 20% above current hearing protection) and selling through direct-to-consumer channels, leveraging its existing brand for credibility.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of Hellberg’s advanced technology and design.; The functional advantage is not currently offered by competitors.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for the advantage.. Predictions: In a test offering a wireless Bluetooth model versus a standard model, purchase intent will be higher for the wireless model among target users.; Willingness to pay will be at least 20% higher for the wireless model compared to the standard model..

T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is positioned as a status or lifestyle accessory, and they are willing to pay a premium for brand prestige and design aesthetics, especially among younger or fashion-conscious segments. Who benefits: Consumers who view hearing protection as a fashion item or status signal, such as young professionals, urban dwellers, or those who follow trendy lifestyle brands.. Why behaviour changes: If a product is perceived as a stylish or aspirational accessory, consumers will purchase it even if the functional benefit is marginal, because it aligns with their self-image and social signaling.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by pricing at a premium (e.g., 20% above current hearing protection) and selling through fashion-focused channels or collaborations with lifestyle brands, leveraging its design heritage.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Hellberg with premium design and innovative technology.; Hearing protection is perceived as a status item or fashion accessory.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for brand prestige and design.. Predictions: In a test offering a stylish, design-focused model versus a standard model, purchase intent will be higher for the design model among fashion-conscious consumers.; Willingness to pay will be at least 20% higher for the design model compared to the standard model..

Test "Wireless vs Status Hearing Protection Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a wireless Bluetooth model (functional advantage) or a status/design-focused model (fashion accessory). They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1–10) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and urban/rural residence.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1–10) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the wireless model.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the status/design model.. Decision rule: If the wireless model’s average willingness to pay is at least 20% higher than the status model, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the status model’s willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 20%, we conclude the evidence is inconclusive.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed 12‑week, €20,000 test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a wireless Bluetooth model versus a status/design model. If the wireless model shows at least 20% higher willingness to pay, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional advantage; otherwise, reconsider expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed 12‑week, €20,000 test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a wireless Bluetooth model versus a status/design model. If the wireless model shows at least 20% higher willingness to pay, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional advantage; otherwise, reconsider expansion. Target customer: Consumers seeking hands‑free hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., outdoor enthusiasts, musicians, or workers) who are willing to pay a premium for convenience and advanced technology.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that offers wireless Bluetooth connectivity, superior comfort, and specific use‑case functionality, positioned as a premium, innovative solution for targeted consumer segments.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 10‑week, €18,000 test (X1) as outlined in the evidence ledger, collect purchase intent and willingness to pay data, and analyze results against the 20% threshold.. Uncertainty: The exact demand for a differentiated proposition is unknown; the test will resolve whether the functional advantage drives willingness to pay.. Would change if: If the test shows the status/design model outperforms the wireless model by at least 20%, we would reconsider a status‑driven proposition.; If additional evidence reveals strong price sensitivity or limited willingness to pay a premium, we would reassess the investment case.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Outdoor Recreation vs Boat Owner Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product pages and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, mountaineers) and 250 boat/aircraft owners (small private boats and recreational aircraft). Recruit via outdoor recreation forums, boating associations, and aviation clubs.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1=Would not buy; 7=Would definitely buy). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (maximum price they would pay).. Predictions: T1: Outdoor recreationists will show purchase intent above 5 (moderately likely to buy) and a willingness to pay at least €200.; T2: Boat and aircraft owners will show purchase intent above 5 (moderately likely to buy) and a willingness to pay at least €300.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for outdoor recreationists is ≥5.5 AND the average willingness to pay is ≥€200, proceed with consumer proposition (supports T1). If the average purchase intent for boat/aircraft owners is ≥5.5 AND the average willingness to pay is ≥€300, proceed with B2B expansion (supports T2). If neither group meets the threshold, abandon the proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay among outdoor recreationists and boat/aircraft owners. If the test meets the 5.5 purchase intent threshold and €200 willingness to pay threshold, proceed to develop a consumer proposition. Otherwise, abandon the proposition and focus on B2B expansion or no expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
